uses: Dandelion root has long been a traditional bitter tonic, taken for sluggish digestion and a poor appetite, and Culpeper credited it with opening the liver and gall. The leaf was used in folk practice to increase urine; Culpeper's name for the plant, piss-a-bed, reflects this. Flowers, leaves and root all have a place in the folk medicine of Mexico, China and North America. In the kitchen, young spring leaves go into salads, the roasted root makes a coffee substitute, and the flowers are made into wine.
taste: Bitter; young spring leaves are milder
energetics: Culpeper called dandelion opening, cleansing and drying
caution_pregnancy: Little is known about safety in more than food amounts during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and the EMA does not recommend medicinal dandelion then. Not enough is known; avoid medicinal amounts. LactMed judges use while nursing unlikely to harm the baby.
caution_medications: Dandelion may add to the effects of diuretics (water pills) and of diabetes medicines that lower blood sugar. NCCIH also lists blood thinners and anti-platelet drugs as possible concerns. In lab and animal studies it changed liver enzymes that break down many drugs, and one kidney transplant patient had toxic levels of immune-suppressing medicine after drinking a tea containing dandelion. Talk to your provider first if you take any of these.
caution_conditions: Avoid it with a blocked bile duct, gallstones, other gallbladder or bile-duct disease, liver disease or an active stomach ulcer. Avoid it with kidney failure, diabetes or heart failure, because it is high in potassium. Do not use it if you are allergic to daisy-family plants such as daisies, marigolds, ragweed or chrysanthemums, though evidence on cross-reactions is mixed. Side effects can include mild diarrhea, heartburn, stomach upset and low blood sugar. Use isn't established for children under 12.
caution_duration: If symptoms last more than 2 weeks, see a doctor or qualified practitioner. Heavy use over months has harmed at least one person: a man with kidney disease who drank many cups a day developed skin damage from high oxalate levels.
caution_topical: The milky sap can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive people, and topical dandelion may trigger allergy in people with eczema (atopic dermatitis). Contact dermatitis from handling the plant may be more common in children.
garden_harvest_timing: Pick leaves young, in early spring before buds appear; they turn bitter later. Dig roots of two-year plants; autumn roots are firmer and hold more stored inulin. Gather flowers early and use them at once, as they close quickly.
garden_water: Grows almost anywhere; its deep taproot rides out drought, though heat and dry spells make the leaves bitter
notes: A short-lived perennial that self-sows freely and regrows from any piece of root left behind. Its early flowers are an important nectar source for bees. Only harvest from ground that hasn't been sprayed, and wash well. Look-alikes such as hawkbit and chicory can be confused with it. Children blow the seed heads to tell the time. Culpeper places dandelion under Jupiter.
